case_analysis.focal_point: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 1512(c)(2) criminalizes any corrupt obstruction of an official proceeding or is instead limited to obstruction acts that impair the integrity or availability of evidence used in that proceeding.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 1512(c), especially § 1512(c)(2) (part of the federal witness/victim/informant tampering and obstruction framework).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Fischer argues that the D.C. Circuit construed § 1512(c)(2) too broadly by treating it as a catchall covering any interference with an official proceeding (including the January 6 electoral-count certification) even when the conduct does not involve evidence impairment. He contends § 1512(c)(2) should be read in context with § 1512(c)(1) and the surrounding witness/evidence-focused provisions, so that (c)(2) reaches only conduct akin to (c)(1)—i.e., acts directed at destroying, altering, concealing, or otherwise impairing documents, records, or other evidence for use in an official proceeding. On this view, applying (c)(2) to non-evidence-related disruption improperly expands a statute labeled and structured around witness/evidence tampering, creating overbreadth and fair-notice concerns.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues that § 1512(c)(2) is textually broader than evidence impairment and independently prohibits corruptly obstructing, influencing, or impeding any official proceeding (or attempting to do so), regardless of whether the means involve documents or other evidence. The government maintains that the D.C. Circuit correctly rejected the effort to limit (c)(2) to evidence-focused conduct; it contends that prior appellate cases upholding (c)(2) convictions do not establish an outer boundary confining the statute to evidence impairment, because those cases did not need to decide that narrower legal limitation. Accordingly, the government asserts that Fischer’s conduct—aimed at stopping or delaying the congressional certification proceeding—falls within (c)(2)’s ordinary scope when done "corruptly."

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point remains the structural one: two numbered paragraphs and broad verbs in (c)(2) can suggest independent scope, and she invokes Loughrin to reinforce that inference. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, “otherwise” is not surplusage; in ordinary usage it signals an alternative means of accomplishing the same general kind of obstruction described in (c)(1), and the surrounding placement in § 1512’s witness/evidence-tampering scheme makes the Government’s free-standing reading an implausibly sweeping expansion in a criminal statute. Loughrin is distinguishable because it did not involve an “otherwise” residual tether immediately following a specific evidentiary prohibition, and here a whole-text reading avoids turning Sarbanes–Oxley’s anti-shredding amendment into a general obstruction code that would crowd out more tailored provisions and raise fair-notice concerns. A narrow holding tethering (c)(2) to evidence-integrity impairment (including non-documentary forms) preserves meaningful coverage without rewriting (c)(2) into either redundancy or boundlessness.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point—separate numbering plus broad verbs aimed at “any official proceeding,” reinforced by § 1515(a)(1)’s definition—cannot overcome the textual connective “otherwise,” which in ordinary usage signals a residual clause tied to the specific kind of obstruction just described in (c)(1). As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, reading (c)(2) as a free-standing obstruction felony would largely nullify (c)(1)’s careful evidentiary specification and, in context of § 1512’s witness/evidence-tampering scheme, would smuggle an “elephant in a mousehole” into Sarbanes–Oxley without clearer textual direction. Loughrin’s structural reasoning, invoked by Justice Sotomayor, is distinguishable because it lacked an “otherwise” bridge that grammatically and conceptually links the paragraphs here, and it does not justify ignoring immediate statutory context. Given the criminal setting, the narrower evidence-impairment-linked reading better fits the text’s original public meaning and avoids expansive liability without clear notice.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s structural point—separate numbering and broad verbs in (c)(2), with an analogy to Loughrin—deserves engagement, but it cannot overcome the textual limiter “otherwise,” which, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch explain, ordinarily functions as a residual tether to the immediately preceding, more specific category of conduct. Loughrin is distinguishable because it lacked this “otherwise” bridge and did not sit inside a witness/evidence-tampering framework like § 1512; here, whole-text context and noscitur a sociis/ejusdem generis strongly indicate Congress meant “otherwise” to capture alternative means of evidence-impairment-type obstruction, not to create a general obstruction felony. Accepting the Government’s broader reading would, in practical consequence, convert a Sarbanes–Oxley anti-shredding amendment into sweeping, unpredictable criminal liability that risks swallowing more tailored obstruction provisions—precisely the sort of expansion that, in a criminal statute, should not be inferred from ambiguous drafting. The narrower construction still leaves (c)(2) meaningful without erasing (c)(1)’s work, and any remaining uncertainty is resolved by restraint and fair-notice principles.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s point that “otherwise” often signals a same-kind residual clause and that § 1512 sits in an evidence/witness-tampering neighborhood, so we should be cautious about turning (c)(2) into an all-purpose obstruction code. But that contextual inference cannot do the work of rewriting enacted text that separately prohibits corruptly obstructing “any official proceeding,” especially given § 1515(a)(1)’s concrete definition that cabins the provision to formal proceedings rather than everyday governmental activity. Justice Gorsuch’s lenity and fair-notice concerns are real, yet the demanding mens rea (“corruptly”) and the proceeding-based limitation meaningfully narrow the statute; by contrast, tethering (c)(2) to evidence-impairment risks leaving serious corrupt interference with core democratic proceedings outside the reach of the paragraph Congress actually wrote. Yates/Begay warn against unmoored residual clauses, but here the object (“official proceeding”) supplies an anchor that avoids both boundlessness and redundancy without collapsing (c)(2) into (c)(1).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s structural point—that separate numbering plus the breadth of “any official proceeding” should give (c)(2) independent scope—is the best case for Respondent, and her invocation of Loughrin usefully reminds us that paragraphing can matter. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, the word “otherwise” is a textual connector that ordinarily signals an alternative means of accomplishing the same general kind of obstruction described in (c)(1), and that contextual cue is stronger here than the structural inference Sotomayor draws from numbering. Loughrin is distinguishable because it did not involve an “otherwise” residual immediately following a specific prohibition; and reading (c)(2) as a free-standing catchall would, as Justice Gorsuch notes, create serious coherence and fair-notice problems by effectively turning a Sarbanes–Oxley evidence-integrity amendment into a general obstruction code. On a pragmatic textualist view, the narrower reading still leaves (c)(2) meaningful (covering other evidence-integrity impairments) while preserving statutory fit across Title 18.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point remains structural: separate numbering plus broad verbs and the defined term “official proceeding” can suggest independent scope, and she analogizes to Loughrin. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, “otherwise” is not surplusage; in ordinary usage it introduces an alternative means of accomplishing the same general kind of obstruction just described, and here (c)(1) is plainly about impairing the integrity/availability of evidence for a proceeding. Loughrin is distinguishable because it did not involve an “otherwise” residual clause immediately following a specific evidentiary prohibition inside a witness/evidence-tampering statute; Yates’s whole-text approach reinforces resisting a reading that converts Sarbanes–Oxley’s targeted anti-shredding amendment into a free-standing, sweeping obstruction felony. Given the competing cues, the narrower, evidence-impairment-linked construction best fits the text-in-context and avoids the fair-notice problems that attend the Government’s boundless reading in a criminal statute.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s structural point—separate numbering and broad verbs in (c)(2), plus her invocation of Loughrin—deserves weight, but it does not overcome the connective force of “otherwise,” which ordinarily signals an alternative means of accomplishing the same general kind of obstruction just described in (c)(1). As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the whole-text context of § 1512 (witness/evidence tampering) and Sarbanes–Oxley’s anti-shredding impetus make it implausible that Congress hid an all-purpose obstruction felony in this subsection (“elephants in mouseholes”), especially given the redundancy and displacement effects across adjacent Title 18 obstruction provisions. Loughrin is distinguishable because it did not involve an “otherwise” residual clause immediately following a specific evidentiary prohibition; here Yates/Begay-style caution against unmoored residual expansions, combined with fair-notice and lenity concerns in criminal law, supports the narrower, evidence-impairment-linked construction. Sotomayor’s mens rea response (“corruptly” plus proceeding limitation) mitigates breadth somewhat, but under an institutionalist, precedent- and coherence-minded approach it is not a sufficient textual anchor to justify the Government’s sweeping reading.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point remains that (c)(2)’s separate numbering and broad proceeding-focused language suggest an independent prohibition, and she is right that § 1515(a)(1)’s definition of “official proceeding” supplies some boundary. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the enacted connector “otherwise” is not surplusage: in ordinary usage and in this immediate syntactic placement, it signals an alternative means of accomplishing the same general kind of obstruction described in (c)(1), which is evidence-impairment. Loughrin’s paragraph-structure inference does not carry the same force here because it did not involve an “otherwise” residual tether immediately following a specific prohibition, and Yates’s contextual approach to Sarbanes–Oxley strengthens, rather than weakens, reading (c)(2) in harmony with § 1512’s evidence/witness-tampering scheme. Given the criminal context, adopting the Government’s free-standing construction would create a sweeping, unpredictable obstruction felony and risk redundancy with (c)(1) and displacement of more tailored Title 18 provisions—an expansion that should require clearer textual signals.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that (c)(2)’s broad verbs, the separate numbering, and the “official proceeding” definition supply an independent, proceeding-focused offense—does not, for me, overcome the limiting work of “otherwise” and the surrounding § 1512 scheme. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, reading (c)(2) as a free-standing catchall risks turning a Sarbanes–Oxley evidence-integrity amendment into a general obstruction felony that creates fair-notice problems and crowds out more tailored Title 18 provisions, a concern reinforced by Yates’s insistence on statutory neighborhood. Loughrin’s structural inference is less persuasive here because the “otherwise” bridge immediately follows a specific evidence-impairment prohibition, making a same-kind residual reading more coherent and administrable. On a pragmatic, fairness-focused approach, the narrower construction still leaves ample tools to punish violent disruption without expanding § 1512(c)(2) in a way that invites unpredictable charging.

John Roberts.reasoning: Read in context, § 1512(c)(2) follows § 1512(c)(1)’s specific evidence-impairment prohibition and sits within a witness/evidence-tampering framework, making it most natural to construe (c)(2) as covering obstructive acts akin to (c)(1) rather than as a free-standing, boundless catchall. Applying canons of contextual reading (noscitur a sociis/related-words reasoning) avoids transforming (c)(2) into a general obstruction statute that would swallow other, more tailored provisions and raise fair-notice concerns in a criminal case. Even if Begay v. United States does not dictate this result, its structural caution against expanding residual-like language beyond its statutory neighborhood supports a narrower construction here, preserving institutional legitimacy by deciding on statutory grounds without reaching broader constitutional questions. I would therefore reverse the D.C. Circuit’s broader reading and hold § 1512(c)(2) limited to obstruction tied to impairing the integrity or availability of evidence for an “official proceeding,” as defined in § 1515(a)(1).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Read in context, § 1512(c)(2) follows § 1512(c)(1)’s specific prohibition on corruptly impairing the integrity or availability of “a record, document, or other object,” and should be construed to reach obstruction of an official proceeding by similar evidence-impairment means rather than as a free-ranging catchall for any disruption. The surrounding provisions of § 1512 are aimed at witness tampering and evidence preservation, and a broader construction risks converting § 1512(c)(2) into a general obstruction statute untethered from the text’s evident focus, raising serious fair-notice concerns. Consistent with Begay v. United States, 553 U.S. 137 (2008), and the related canons of noscitur a sociis/ejusdem generis, “otherwise” in (c)(2) is best read to cover other forms of corrupt evidence-related obstruction not enumerated in (c)(1), rather than to swallow the statute’s limiting context. Because the government’s reading effectively expands federal power beyond what Congress enacted and makes (c)(1) largely redundant, the narrower, text-and-structure-based construction should prevail.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1512(c) must be read as a coherent unit: (c)(1) targets impairment of “a record, document, or other object,” and (c)(2)’s “otherwise obstructs, influences, or impedes any official proceeding” is best understood, under ordinary contextual reading and the limiting force of “otherwise,” to reach obstruction accomplished by means akin to (c)(1)’s evidence-impairment conduct rather than to create an unlimited catchall. Reading (c)(2) as the Government proposes would detach it from the surrounding witness-and-evidence-tampering framework and create sweeping federal criminal liability with serious fair-notice and overbreadth consequences—concerns that counsel restraint in construing ambiguous criminal statutes. The canons of noscitur a sociis and ejusdem generis, as applied in cases like Yates, reinforce that a broad residual phrase should be tethered to its specific neighbors in a tightly drawn list. A narrower construction also avoids turning § 1512(c)(2) into a de facto “general obstruction” statute when Congress has elsewhere enacted more targeted obstruction provisions.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1512(c)(2) independently prohibits anyone who “corruptly… obstructs, influences, or impedes any official proceeding,” and that ordinary language is not naturally confined to document- or evidence-impairment covered by § 1512(c)(1). Congress’s decision to separate (c)(1) and (c)(2) into distinct, numbered paragraphs supports giving (c)(2) independent scope rather than treating it as mere surplusage, as this Court emphasized when similar structural cues signaled distinct reach in Loughrin v. United States, 573 U.S. 351, 359 (2014). While Yates v. United States, 574 U.S. 528 (2015), shows that context can narrow a catchall, § 1512(c)(2)’s text and structure do not fit ejusdem generis/noscitur a sociis in the same way, and the definition of “official proceeding” in § 1515(a)(1) confirms Congress targeted obstruction of proceedings themselves. Reading (c)(2) to reach corrupt efforts to halt the electoral-count certification aligns with the statute’s protective purpose and avoids undercutting accountability for conduct that threatens core democratic processes and public safety.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Read in context, § 1512(c)(2) follows immediately after (c)(1)’s detailed evidence-impairment prohibition and sits within a statute largely organized around witness- and evidence-related obstruction; applying noscitur a sociis/ejusdem generis to that structure supports limiting (c)(2) to conduct that, like (c)(1), targets the integrity or availability of evidence for use in an "official proceeding." The government’s broader reading risks turning (c)(2) into a sweeping, free-standing obstruction statute that crowds out neighboring provisions and creates incoherence within the § 1512 scheme, while a narrower construction preserves workable boundaries and fair notice without rendering (c)(2) superfluous (it still captures non-documentary evidence impairment and comparable means). Begay v. United States underscores the Court’s caution about untethered residual-style clauses and reinforces reading broad language in light of its statutory neighbors to avoid indeterminate, expansive constructions. Under § 1515(a)(1)’s definition of "official proceeding," the proceeding may be covered, but the means criminalized by (c)(2) should remain evidence-impairment-like rather than any disruption writ large.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1512(c) must be read as a coherent whole: (c)(1) targets impairing “a record, document, or other object,” and (c)(2)’s residual phrase “otherwise obstructs, influences, or impedes” is best understood—using ordinary interpretive tools like noscitur a sociis/ejusdem generis—to cover obstructive acts of the same general kind, i.e., those aimed at evidence integrity or availability for an “official proceeding.” Reading (c)(2) as a free-standing, all-purpose obstruction felony risks turning a targeted evidence-tampering provision enacted in Sarbanes–Oxley into an unbounded catchall, raising fair-notice concerns and inviting prosecutors to do work Congress has assigned elsewhere, contrary to separation-of-powers principles. Where the government’s broader construction would dramatically expand criminal liability beyond the statute’s evident focus and create serious ambiguity at the margins, the rule of lenity counsels the narrower reading. Consistent with Yates v. United States’ contextual reading of Sarbanes–Oxley’s broad language by reference to neighboring terms, (c)(2) should not be stretched to reach obstruction untethered from evidence impairment.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1512(c) must be read as a coherent whole: subsection (c)(1) squarely targets document/evidence impairment, and subsection (c)(2)’s use of “otherwise” is most naturally understood to cover other obstructive acts of the same general kind, not to create a free-standing, virtually unlimited obstruction statute for “any” interference with an official proceeding. Reading (c)(2) as a broad catchall risks collapsing distinct obstruction provisions across Title 18, creating serious fair-notice and workability problems and pushing major new criminal liability into a statute situated in an evidence- and witness-tampering framework—an “elephants in mouseholes” concern. Although Begay v. United States did not dictate a particular reading of “otherwise,” its structural approach supports using context and statutory structure to cabin broad residual language rather than treating it as an all-purpose sweep. Given the statute’s history and the need for a restrained, precedent-consistent construction in criminal law, I would limit § 1512(c)(2) to conduct that, like (c)(1), impairs the integrity or availability of evidence for use in an official proceeding.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1512(c) is a two-part provision enacted in an evidence-tampering statute; reading (c)(2) as a free-standing catchall for any interference with an official proceeding risks collapsing (c)(1)’s specific focus on documents and other evidence and diluting the limiting work done by the word “otherwise.” Applying the whole-text canon and ejusdem generis/noscitur a sociis, (c)(2) is best read to reach obstructive acts akin to (c)(1)—i.e., conduct that corruptly impairs the integrity or availability of evidence for use in an “official proceeding.” This narrower reading is reinforced by this Court’s approach to similar residual language in Begay v. United States, 553 U.S. 137, 143 (2008), and by Yates v. United States, 574 U.S. 528 (2015), which rejected an “unrestrained” reading of Sarbanes-Oxley’s evidence-related terms divorced from their statutory context. Precedent does not compel a broader construction where prior cases upheld convictions without deciding whether (c)(2) extends beyond evidence-impairment conduct, and methodological consistency favors the contextual, text-based limitation.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Reading § 1512(c)(2) in context with § 1512(c)(1) and the surrounding witness/evidence-tampering scheme, the more coherent construction is that (c)(2) reaches obstruction that, like (c)(1), targets the integrity or availability of evidence for use in an “official proceeding.” Construing (c)(2) as a free-standing, all-purpose obstruction statute risks collapsing distinct obstruction provisions across Title 18, expanding federal criminal liability in a way that raises serious fair-notice concerns and invites overcharging—concerns this Court has taken seriously when general language is yoked to a more specific list. Applying the contextual canons reflected in Yates v. United States, 574 U.S. 528 (2015), and consistent with Aguilar-style caution about overbroad obstruction theories, I would avoid transforming Sarbanes–Oxley’s targeted anti-shredding amendment into a sweeping catchall. That narrower reading still leaves ample tools for prosecuting violent disruption and other misconduct (e.g., assault, trespass, or conspiracy statutes) without stretching § 1512(c)(2) beyond its evidentiary core.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 1512(c)(2) criminalizes any corrupt obstruction of an official proceeding or is instead limited to obstruction that impairs the integrity or availability of evidence for use in that proceeding.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 1512(c)(2) (part of the federal witness tampering/obstruction statute)
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Fischer argues the D.C. Circuit construed § 1512(c)(2) too broadly by treating it as a sweeping, stand-alone obstruction offense covering conduct unrelated to evidence; he contends subsection (c)(2) must be read in context with § 1512(c)(1) and the surrounding evidence-focused provisions, so that (c)(2) reaches only conduct that obstructs an official proceeding through evidence impairment (e.g., altering, destroying, concealing, or otherwise compromising evidence or its availability/integrity).
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues § 1512(c)(2) is not limited to evidence impairment and instead covers any conduct that 'corruptly' obstructs, influences, or impedes an official proceeding (including Congress’s electoral-vote certification), and that prior appellate decisions upholding convictions under § 1512(c)(2) do not establish an evidence-only boundary; rather, those cases applied the statute to their facts and do not foreclose broader applications.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—the shift in (c)(2) to proceeding-directed verbs and the object “any official proceeding”—cannot be ignored, and it is the best textual case for a freestanding obstruction offense. But as Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, “otherwise” functions as a genuine connector in this sentence, and reading it to launch a general obstruction felony untethered to (c)(1)’s evidentiary focus sits uneasily with § 1512’s immediate neighborhood and Sarbanes–Oxley’s targeted design (a Yates-style contextual cue). Justice Kagan’s reliance on Ali does affect my analysis by cautioning against contrived narrowing, yet here the limitation comes from the statute’s residual-clause structure itself rather than atextual policy concerns, and some overlap with (c)(1) is not enough to defeat the more coherent, cabined reading. I therefore stay with petitioner on a narrow holding: (c)(2) reaches corrupt obstruction of an official proceeding when accomplished through impairing the integrity or availability of evidence (or analogous process inputs), without deciding the outer boundary beyond that context.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is the grammatical shift in (c)(2) to verbs aimed at “any official proceeding,” which—read in isolation—sounds like an independent, proceeding-focused prohibition. But under a textualist reading attentive to ordinary usage and statutory structure, the connective “otherwise” most naturally links (c)(2) to the kind of obstruction described in (c)(1), especially given § 1512’s surrounding focus on evidence and witness integrity; that linkage provides the statute’s limiting principle more faithfully than relying on the indeterminate term “corruptly,” as Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch emphasize. Ali does not compel the broad reading Justice Kagan urges because the narrowing here is not atextual: it follows from the residual-clause form and placement, much as Yates instructed courts to read Sarbanes–Oxley’s broad words in context rather than letting them swallow the scheme. The redundancy concern does not defeat this interpretation; overlap is common, and (c)(2) still reaches other corrupt, evidence-impairing methods not captured by (c)(1)’s enumerated verbs, with lenity as a backstop if doubt remains.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The strongest petitioner point, pressed by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett, is that “otherwise” ordinarily links (c)(2) to (c)(1) and that § 1512’s neighborhood is evidence/witness-centered, with Yates counseling contextual narrowing in Sarbanes–Oxley. But that cannot be the end of the textual analysis where Congress altered the object from “a record, document, or other object” to “any official proceeding” and used proceeding-directed verbs (“obstructs, influences, or impedes”), choices that are hard to square with an evidence-only residual clause without effectively rewriting (c)(2) to track (c)(1). Justice Gorsuch’s and Justice Jackson’s fair-notice/lenity concerns are serious, yet I do not find the statute grievously ambiguous once the distinct grammar is given effect; the narrowing work is better done by a demanding construction of “corruptly” rather than by collapsing (c)(2) into a near-duplicate of (c)(1). Ali’s caution against artificially narrowing broad, coherent text remains more apt here than importing an ejusdem generis limitation that drains the independent function Congress appeared to add.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch press the strongest point for petitioner: “otherwise” commonly functions as a residual connector, and § 1512’s neighborhood is evidence- and witness-centric, so an ejusdem generis limit may seem to preserve coherence and fair notice. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Alito note, Congress deliberately changed the object from “a record, document, or other object” in (c)(1) to “any official proceeding” in (c)(2) and used proceeding-directed verbs; importing an evidence-only object is less contextual reading than effectively rewriting the actus reus to avoid a breadth concern. Yates’s contextual caution matters, yet it addressed linguistically awkward overbreadth (“tangible object”) tied to a noun list, while here (c)(2) is grammatically coherent on its face; the more principled constraint—consistent with my criminal-justice methodology—is a demanding construction of “corruptly,” not shrinking (c)(2) into near-duplication of (c)(1). Lenity, as Justice Gorsuch invokes, is a backstop only after ambiguity persists, and I do not see that residual ambiguity once we give effect to the distinct object and verbs Congress chose.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Barrett’s strongest point is that “otherwise” commonly signals a residual clause linked to the prior example, and § 1512’s neighborhood is evidence-and-witness oriented; that contextual pull is real. But the petitioner’s approach still requires overriding the most salient textual shift Congress made—changing the object from “a record, document, or other object” in (c)(1) to “any official proceeding” in (c)(2) and pairing it with proceeding-directed verbs—so an evidence-only gloss risks collapsing (c)(2) into (c)(1) rather than giving each clause coherent work. Yates (invoked by Roberts/Barrett/Thomas) rightly demands contextual discipline, yet it involved a broad noun (“tangible object”) that became awkward outside its list; here (c)(2)’s syntax is straightforward and self-contained, and context can be honored by reading “corruptly” as a stringent constraint on proceeding-interference rather than by rewriting the actus reus. Justice Gorsuch’s lenity concern is consequential only if genuine ambiguity remains after accounting for that distinct grammatical structure, and on my pragmatic textualism the better reading is that (c)(2) reaches corrupt obstruction of the proceeding itself.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor press the strongest point against my view: (c)(2)’s shift to “any official proceeding” and proceeding-directed verbs reads naturally as a free-standing obstruction offense, and an evidence-limited construction risks near-overlap with (c)(1). But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, the word “otherwise” is a real textual hinge; in ordinary grammar it signals a residual clause tethered to the same genus of misconduct just described, and § 1512’s surrounding provisions overwhelmingly concern witness/evidence integrity, making an ejusdem generis reading the best fit for the statute as enacted. Justice Alito’s invocation of Ali does not move me because Ali cautions against narrowing clear terms in isolation, whereas the ambiguity here arises from the residual-clause structure and statutory neighborhood—precisely the situation where contextual canons (and, if needed, lenity and fair-notice principles) properly constrain an overbroad criminal construction. The narrower reading still gives (c)(2) independent work—capturing other corrupt methods of impairing evidence availability or integrity affecting an official proceeding—even if it does not become a general-purpose obstruction felony.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Alito press the strongest point for respondent: (c)(2) switches from evidence-focused objects to “any official proceeding,” paired with proceeding-directed verbs, and we should be wary of reading (c)(2) as redundant. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett are right that “otherwise” is a relational term that ordinarily links the residual clause to the kind of obstruction just described, and § 1512’s surrounding provisions overwhelmingly concern protecting evidence and witness integrity for use in proceedings—context that, under Yates-style reasoning, informs the scope of the residual phrase. On their reading, (c)(2) still does real work by covering corrupt evidence-impairment schemes that do not neatly fit (c)(1)’s enumerated verbs, while avoiding converting this targeted Sarbanes–Oxley amendment into a general-purpose obstruction felony. I remain unpersuaded by Justice Sotomayor’s suggestion that “corruptly” can do the limiting alone; in criminal law it is too indeterminate to justify the breadth respondent seeks where the connective and statutory setting point narrower.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is the grammatical shift in (c)(2) to proceeding-directed verbs and the object “any official proceeding,” which on first read supports a freestanding obstruction offense and raises a surplusage concern if we over-cabin the clause. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, “otherwise” is not decorative; in ordinary usage it signals a residual clause keyed to the kind of misconduct just described, and in § 1512’s evidence-and-witness-tampering architecture that relational term fairly narrows (c)(2) to other corrupt means of impairing evidence integrity or availability for a proceeding. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Ali does not move me because Ali’s anti-narrowing principle applies when the text is clear in isolation, whereas here the residual-clause connective and placement generate the ambiguity; and “corruptly,” as Justice Jackson notes, is too elastic to serve as the principal limiter for a sweeping construction in a criminal statute. The overlap concern does not defeat the narrower reading because (c)(2) still covers obstructive, evidence-impairing schemes that evade (c)(1)’s enumerated verbs, while avoiding turning (c)(2) into a general obstruction felony without clearer congressional direction.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that (c)(2)’s shift to the object “any official proceeding,” paired with proceeding-directed verbs, reads naturally as an independent obstruction offense and avoids collapsing into (c)(1). But under my pragmatic, criminal-law fairness lens, that textual intuition does not overcome the structural signal Justice Barrett and the Chief emphasize: “otherwise” is a relational connector that reasonably invites an ejusdem generis constraint tied to the type of obstruction just described, and § 1512’s immediate neighborhood reinforces an evidence-and-witness-integrity focus. I also remain unpersuaded by Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on “corruptly” as the principal limiting principle; as Justice Kavanaugh notes, it is too elastic to provide reliable notice and administrable bounds if (c)(2) becomes a general-purpose obstruction felony. Ali’s admonition (raised by Justice Alito) against narrowing broad text matters, but here any narrowing comes from the statute’s own connective structure rather than atextual policy trimming, and that makes the petitioner’s reading the better fit in a criminal statute.

John Roberts.reasoning: Read in context, § 1512(c)(2) follows § 1512(c)(1)’s detailed evidence-tampering prohibition and is best understood—under the ordinary contextual canons—to reach other corrupt acts that similarly obstruct an official proceeding by impairing the integrity or availability of evidence, rather than creating a free-floating obstruction offense. Although the Government is right that “otherwise” can introduce a catchall, adopting its sweeping construction would markedly expand § 1512(c)(2) beyond the evidence-centered structure of § 1512 as a whole and raise serious notice and overbreadth concerns, counsels for a narrower construction where text and context permit. Begay’s residual-clause analysis is not directly controlling, but its use of contextual limitation reinforces the point that broad catchall language should be confined by neighboring, more specific terms when Congress has legislated in a targeted field. A narrow ruling preserves institutional legitimacy and respects the statute’s design, leaving broader obstruction policy choices to Congress rather than judicial enlargement of § 1512(c)(2).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Read in context and according to ordinary meaning, § 1512(c)(2)’s residual phrase (“otherwise obstructs, influences, or impedes”) is best limited by the neighboring, evidence-centered prohibition in § 1512(c)(1), with “otherwise” signaling a similar mode of obstruction rather than creating a free-standing, all-purpose obstruction offense. Applying noscitur a sociis and ejusdem generis, as this Court did to constrain a broad catchall in Sarbanes–Oxley in Yates v. United States, supports construing (c)(2) to reach obstruction that impairs the integrity or availability of evidence for use in an “official proceeding,” not any interference with a proceeding writ large. A contrary reading would convert § 1512(c)(2) into a sweeping general obstruction statute despite Congress placing it within a targeted witness-tampering/evidence-preservation scheme and would risk duplicating or displacing more specific obstruction provisions. Because text and structure, not policy concerns, control, I would adopt the narrower, evidence-impairment construction urged by Fischer.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of 18 U.S.C. § 1512(c)(2) makes it a separate offense to “otherwise obstruct[], influence[], or impede[] any official proceeding,” and that broad language is not naturally limited to evidence-impairment when Congress added the explicit evidence-focused conduct in § 1512(c)(1). The ejusdem generis/noscitur a sociis canons do not overcome the ordinary meaning here because (c)(2) is not a vague catchall tacked onto a narrow list of similar items; it uses distinct verbs directed to the proceeding itself, and reading it to reach only evidence impairment risks rendering (c)(2) largely duplicative of (c)(1). As in Ali v. Federal Bureau of Prisons, 552 U.S. 214 (2008), we should not artificially narrow broad statutory language based on surrounding terms absent genuine textual ambiguity, and practical consequences counsel against creating an evidence-only loophole for corrupt interference with Congress’s proceedings. Yates v. United States, 574 U.S. 528 (2015) (Alito, J., concurring) illustrates that context-based narrowing applies where an expansive reading produces grammatical or structural incoherence, but § 1512(c)(2) remains coherent and operative when read to cover non-evidence obstruction so long as the Government proves the “corruptly” mens rea.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1512(c)(2) prohibits whoever “otherwise obstructs, influences, or impedes any official proceeding” when done “corruptly,” and the statute’s definition of “official proceeding” in § 1515(a)(1) is not limited to evidence-gathering tribunals; reading (c)(2) as evidence-only would unnaturally narrow that broad text and risk leaving serious non-evidence obstructions unaddressed. The canons of noscitur a sociis and ejusdem generis do not compel an evidence-impairment limitation here because (c)(2) is a distinct clause with different verbs and objects than (c)(1), unlike the kind of tightly themed list construed in Yates v. United States (2015). This construction also best serves practical fairness and the protection of vulnerable democratic participants by ensuring the law reaches corrupt interference with Congress’s certification proceeding without requiring a contrived showing of evidence tampering. Any overbreadth concern is mitigated by the statute’s demanding mens rea—“corruptly”—which narrows liability to wrongful, blameworthy obstruction rather than ordinary protest or mistake.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1512(c)(2) makes it a crime to “otherwise obstruct[], influence[], or impede[] any official proceeding,” and that broad, operative language—qualified by the mens rea requirement “corruptly”—naturally reaches obstructive conduct beyond evidence impairment. While petitioner invokes noscitur a sociis/ejusdem generis based on (c)(1)’s focus on “record, document, or other object,” those canons do not overcome the text’s residual phrasing and structure; as Begay v. United States cautioned, “otherwise” can, but need not, be read to require similarity to preceding specifics. Reading (c)(2) to cover non-evidence obstruction also better serves statutory coherence and workability by capturing corrupt interferences with “official proceeding[s]” that do not depend on proof of evidence tampering, while the “corruptly” limitation supplies a meaningful narrowing principle. The D.C. Circuit’s contrary reliance on punctuation/line-break distinctions is less persuasive than the straightforward reading of the statutory sentence as enacted.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1512(c) is a single sentence split into two subsections, and subsection (c)(2)’s residual phrase (“otherwise obstructs, influences, or impedes any official proceeding”) is best read in light of (c)(1)’s specific focus on altering, destroying, mutilating, or concealing “a record, document, or other object” for use in an official proceeding. Applying noscitur a sociis and ejusdem generis, we avoid letting the word “otherwise” give the statute ‘unintended breadth’ untethered from the evidence-impairment nucleus of § 1512, as this Court has cautioned in Williams, 553 U.S. 285, 294 (2008), and Gustafson, 513 U.S. 561, 575 (1995), and as reflected in Yates, 574 U.S. 528, 545 (2015) (plurality). Reading (c)(2) as a sweeping, stand-alone obstruction crime would risk collapsing distinct obstruction provisions Congress enacted elsewhere and would raise fair-notice concerns in a criminal statute—concerns that should be resolved, at minimum, by the rule of lenity. The more faithful textual and structural reading therefore limits § 1512(c)(2) to obstructive acts that impair the integrity or availability of evidence for use in an official proceeding.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Read in context, § 1512(c)(2) should be construed in light of § 1512(c)(1) and the surrounding, evidence-centered structure of § 1512, which repeatedly targets tampering with “records, documents, or other objects” and their availability for proceedings. The residual language in (c)(2) is best understood as covering other corrupt means of obstructing a proceeding that are akin to (c)(1)’s evidence-impairment focus, rather than creating a sweeping, stand-alone obstruction offense that would federalize a wide range of conduct and raise serious workability and notice concerns. Consistent with the Court’s approach in Yates v. United States (2015), canons such as noscitur a sociis/ejusdem generis support narrowing broad catchall language by reference to its statutory neighbors, especially where a broader reading risks redundancy and overbreadth. Given the importance of clear lines in criminal statutes, the narrower, evidence-impairment construction better fits text, history, and practical administrability while avoiding an expansive reading with uncertain limits.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Reading § 1512(c) as a whole, paragraph (c)(2) follows (c)(1)’s detailed evidence-tampering offense and is introduced by “otherwise,” a textual cue that (c)(2) is best understood to capture other means of accomplishing the same kind of obstruction—i.e., impairing the integrity or availability of evidence for use in an “official proceeding,” rather than creating a free-standing, all-purpose obstruction statute. That construction is reinforced by statutory context: § 1512 is an evidence- and witness-focused scheme, and the government’s broad reading would risk making § 1512(c)(2) swallow neighboring, more tailored obstruction provisions, contrary to ordinary principles against surplusage and in favor of coherent structure. Begay’s use of context to limit a broad residual phrase illustrates that catchall language can be constrained by surrounding specifics and structure, even if Begay’s exact reasoning does not mechanically control here. Precedent such as United States v. Sutherland and United States v. Gordon does not compel the government’s sweeping interpretation because those decisions applied (c)(2) on their facts and do not resolve the precise limiting question presented.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Reading § 1512(c) as a whole, subsection (c)(2)’s “otherwise obstructs, influences, or impedes” is best understood to operate in the same evidentiary neighborhood as (c)(1), which expressly targets altering, destroying, or concealing “a record, document, or other object” used in an “official proceeding.” Applying ejusdem generis/noscitur a sociis—as this Court did to narrow Sarbanes-Oxley’s broad language in Yates v. United States—counsels against converting (c)(2) into a sweeping, free-standing obstruction felony untethered to evidence, especially given the serious practical consequences and fair-notice concerns in criminal law. That narrower construction preserves procedural fairness and avoids overbreadth by channeling prosecutions for non-evidence obstruction into more tailored statutes, while still reaching corrupt evidence-impairment schemes that threaten the integrity of proceedings. Begay v. United States supports the interpretive approach of reading a broad residual phrase in light of the specific terms that precede it, reinforcing that “otherwise” can connote similarity rather than limitless expansion.
